slides.title: South Korea's real estate prices are heavily influenced by government housing policies.
text: South Korea's real estate prices are heavily influenced by government housing policies.
However, these policies change dozens of times under each administration, and most people struggle to understand how these changes affect the housing market.
Even policymakers often fail to fully understand the complex economic factors and public psychology that shape the real estate market, leading to policies that fail to achieve their intended goals.

slides.title: Housing policy tools change in rapid succession
text: Housing policy tools change in rapid succession
Recent measures have combined area designations, lending rules and housing supply policies.
Policymakers need to assess policy combinations and timing, alongside individual tools.
Sources: Seoul (Feb 2025), joint ministries (Mar 2025), MOLIT and FSC (Jun, Sep, Oct 2025 and Apr 2026).
notes: Recent changes have repeatedly adjusted area designations, lending, supply and taxes, rather than a single rule.

slides.title: Targeted rules can have different effects in nearby areas
text: Targeted rules can have different effects in nearby areas
Retrospective estimates for the 2020 land transaction permit zones in Jamsil, Samseong, Daechi and Cheongdam.
Rules may stabilize the target area while shifting demand to nearby areas.
These estimates cannot be applied directly to other periods or the entire capital region.
Source: KDI Research Report 2023-06, Housing Markets and Regulation. Estimates apply to specific designations in Seoul.
notes: KDI estimated the effects of land transaction permit requirements introduced in June 2020 in Jamsil, Samseong, Daechi and Cheongdam.
Sales volume in regulated areas fell by 38.3% and prices fell by 4.3%. Prices of nearby unregulated homes rose by 2.3% relative to more distant unregulated homes.
These are retrospective estimates for a specific place and period. They should not be applied directly to a new policy scenario.
Source: https://www.kdi.re.kr/research/reportView?pub_no=18385

slides.title: Policy effects depend on rates, timing and household finances
text: Policy effects depend on rates, timing and household finances
The same rule can have different effects across market conditions and household groups.
Results include sign restrictions in the VAR model
Cash and policy loan eligibility change where they can afford to buy.
The same rate change can mean larger repayment burdens and spending cuts.
Sale timing and extra loan conditions can delay a move.
Loan renewals, taxes and rental terms interact.
A 1 pp DSR rise slowed annual consumption by 0.37% on average, with large differences across groups.
Sources: BOK Issue Notes 2025-26 and 2022-45. Figures depend on each study's sample and model assumptions.
notes: Bank of Korea analysis shows that the sequencing of monetary and macroprudential policies matters.
A 25 bp rate cut was associated with an average one-year response of 1.4% for Seoul apartment prices and 1.2% for mortgage lending.
Early macroprudential tightening reduced loan growth pressure by about 0.4 percentage points. Tightening 4-6 months later reduced it by around 0.2 percentage points.
The VAR identification includes sign restrictions. Do not count the direction of these results again as independent causal evidence.
Policy mix research: https://www.bok.or.kr/portal/bbs/P0002353/view.do?depth=200433&menuNo=200433&nttId=10093611
Household consumption research: https://www.bok.or.kr/portal/bbs/P0002353/view.do?menuNo=2004&nttId=10074253

slides.title: Key questions for policy impact assessment
text: Key questions for policy impact assessment
Policymakers are the primary users. Individuals can explore changes in their buying power and options.
Assess target areas and demand shifts to nearby areas together.
Compare exposure by income, debt, home ownership and policy loan eligibility.
Connect borrowing capacity, transactions, expectations and supply delays.
Check whether each study's location, period and method fit the scenario.
notes: Policymakers are the main users. SweetHome provides evidence for comparing policy scope, exemptions and implementation timing, while leaving decisions to people.
Individuals can use the same model to understand changes in their borrowing capacity and affordable locations.

slides.title: A reviewable workflow from policy document to scenario
text: A reviewable workflow from policy document to scenario
Upload a document, verify the extracted change, set assumptions and compare the resulting constraints.
notes: Current implementation: PolicyWorkflow.tsx, PolicyExperimentView.tsx and policy_pipeline.py.
Text, text-based PDF and HWPX parsing are implemented. Legacy HWP and scanned PDFs require conversion or OCR.
Gemini extraction runs only when GEMINI_API_KEY and GEMINI_MODEL are configured. A limited rules-based engine is also available.
Users confirm one rule, its quoted text, applicable regions, effective date and household or supply inputs. Price sensitivity coefficients are assumptions, not calibrated estimates.

The implementation uses React, FastAPI, local JSON data and browser-local graph drafts. Document AI, Spanner Graph and BigQuery are not claimed as active integrations. Cloud deployment was not verified.

slides.title: A knowledge graph people can inspect and edit
text: A knowledge graph people can inspect and edit
Search nodes, inspect sources and edit relationships without code. Undo changes or exchange JSON drafts.
Actual prototype screenshot. 118 nodes and 318 relationships. Edits stay in this browser and do not update simulations or the server.
notes: Actual local prototype, inspected 16 Oct 2026.
KnowledgeGraph.tsx and graph-editor.ts provide search, local node and edge editing, undo, redo, and JSON import/export.
Drafts use localStorage. No server write, collaborative editing or automatic simulation recalculation is implemented.
The graph contains synthetic policies and research claims. Connections are hypotheses, not proven causal links.

slides.title: What users can inspect and change today
text: What users can inspect and change today
The prototype separates observed data, reviewed policy inputs and assumption-based calculations.
Load an official example or upload text, PDF or HWPX. Review the quoted numerical change. Confirm dates, regions and eligible households before running one-rule experiments.
Gemini is optional and requires configuration
View 77 capital-region boundaries from SGIS 2018 and 30 official Seoul transaction records. Filter area and cancellations. Samples do not represent the whole market.
Compare lending and permit conditions. Hover over LTV, DSR, DTI and rate spreads for definitions. Inspect research sources, conflicting findings and limits.
Source links and terminology at the point of use
Scope as inspected on 16 Oct 2026. Historical demo outcomes and new policy experiments are distinct workflows.
notes: Verified against current source code and the running local prototype on 16 Oct 2026.
Data scope: data/public/README.md. There are 77 SGIS 2018 boundaries and 30 official transaction records from three Seoul districts and two contract dates.
Public records are reference observations and do not calibrate the scenario coefficients.
Definitions: GlossaryHelp.tsx and glossary-data.ts. Policy comparisons: PolicyFactors.tsx.

slides.title: Traceable experiments, with explicit limits
text: Document extraction supports human review. Deterministic calculations expose their inputs and formulas.
No causal price forecast: sensitivities depend on user inputs. Graph edits do not update the server or recalculate scenarios.
notes: Current calculation and disclosure behavior: policy_pipeline.py and PolicyExperimentView.tsx.
Price sensitivity is a user-assumption calculation, not a validated causal forecast or a statistical confidence interval.
Graph source: API demonstration graph, 118 nodes and 318 edges. Edits live in browser localStorage, support undo and JSON exchange, and do not mutate server data or simulation outputs.
Remaining gaps include complete policy coverage, representative data, calibrated regional price effects and collaborative approval.
